summary: This unit covers the microbes that infect the brain, meninges, and nerves: the meningitis bacteria, the two clostridial neurotoxins, the neurotropic viruses, the CNS fungi, and the spirochetes and leprosy bacillus. Exam questions give a patient and a clue (a stain, an exposure, a vector, a toxin effect) and ask which organism or virulence factor explains it.

notes.h: Meningitis bacteria in children and adults
points: Streptococcus pneumoniae: gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci, alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive; the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults.
Its polysaccharide capsule blocks phagocytosis; pneumolysin and IgA protease add to damage.
Neisseria meningitidis: gram-negative diplococci, spread by respiratory droplets in crowded groups such as dorms and military barracks.
Its capsule resists complement, and lipooligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin drives septic shock, petechiae, DIC, and adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).
Deficiency of terminal complement (C5 to C9) raises the risk of repeated Neisseria infection.
Haemophilus influenzae type b: gram-negative coccobacillus with a polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule; needs factors X (hematin) and V (NAD) to grow.
Hib conjugate vaccine links PRP to a protein so infants make a T-cell-dependent antibody response; Hib meningitis is now mainly seen in unvaccinated children.
Streptococcus agalactiae (group B): gram-positive cocci in chains, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant; colonizes the maternal vagina and rectum and passes to the baby at birth.
Escherichia coli with the K1 capsule: the K1 polysaccharide resists phagocytosis and complement and helps the bacteria reach the meninges.
Listeria monocytogenes: gram-positive rod, tumbling motility, grows in the refrigerator; found in unpasteurized dairy and deli meats.
Listeria lives inside cells: listeriolysin O lets it escape the phagosome, and ActA builds actin tails that push it into the next cell without meeting antibody.
Listeria crosses the placenta and targets neonates, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weak cell-mediated immunity.
Both toxins are zinc proteases that cleave SNARE proteins, so synaptic vesicles cannot fuse and release transmitter.
Botulinum toxin acts at peripheral cholinergic terminals and blocks acetylcholine release, causing descending flaccid paralysis.
Botulism signs: diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dilated pupils, then descending weakness. Adults eat preformed toxin in canned food; infants swallow spores (honey) that make toxin in the gut.
Tetanospasmin from Clostridium tetani spores in a wound enters motor nerve terminals and travels retrograde to the spinal cord.
There it blocks GABA and glycine release from inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), so motor neurons fire unchecked: trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonos, spastic paralysis.
Herpesviruses: enveloped dsDNA, envelope from the nuclear membrane; they ride axons back to sensory ganglia, stay latent, and travel out again on reactivation.
HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion and causes temporal lobe encephalitis; VZV is latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and reactivates as dermatomal zoster.
JC polyomavirus: nonenveloped circular dsDNA, latent in the kidney; with AIDS or other immunosuppression it infects oligodendrocytes and causes PML.
Enteroviruses (coxsackievirus, echovirus, poliovirus): nonenveloped positive-sense picornaviruses spread fecal-oral, mostly summer and fall; the top cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis.
West Nile virus: enveloped positive-sense flavivirus; Culex mosquitoes carry it from bird reservoirs; humans and horses are dead-end hosts.

Rabies: bullet-shaped, enveloped, negative-sense rhabdovirus; binds the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the bite site and climbs to the CNS by retrograde (dynein) axonal transport. Negri bodies sit in Purkinje and hippocampal neurons.

Cryptococcus neoformans: yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule, in pigeon droppings; inhaled, then spreads to the meninges in AIDS. India ink shows a clear halo; latex agglutination detects capsular antigen.
Mucor and Rhizopus: broad, ribbon-like nonseptate hyphae branching at wide angles; ketoacidosis (acid pH, high glucose, free iron) lets them invade vessels from the sinuses into the orbit and brain.
Coccidioides: dimorphic; mold with arthroconidia in southwestern US desert soil, spherules full of endospores in tissue; can cause chronic basilar meningitis.

Treponema pallidum: thin spirochete too narrow to see on Gram stain; darkfield shows it in a chancre; VDRL and RPR detect nonspecific anticardiolipin antibody; FTA-ABS detects specific antibody and stays positive for life.
Borrelia burgdorferi: spirochete spread by Ixodes ticks (white-footed mouse reservoir, deer host); causes facial palsy and lymphocytic meningitis.
Mycobacterium leprae: acid-fast, cannot be grown in culture, prefers cooler sites (skin, nose, peripheral nerves) and invades Schwann cells; armadillos are a US reservoir.

tricks.label: Please SHiNE my SKiS
tricks.text: Encapsulated bacteria: Pseudomonas, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, N. meningitidis, E. coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella, group B Strep. Asplenia raises the risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria, especially S. pneumoniae, Hib, and N. meningitidis.

tricks.label: Botulism blocks, tetanus tightens
tricks.text: Botulinum stops acetylcholine at the muscle, so muscles go limp. Tetanus toxin stops the brakes (GABA and glycine) in the cord, so muscles lock up.

tricks.label: Both directions on the axon
tricks.text: Rabies and tetanus toxin go retrograde toward the CNS. Herpesviruses go retrograde to reach the ganglion, then anterograde back to the skin when they reactivate.

tricks.label: Ketoacidosis plus black eschar
tricks.text: A patient in DKA with sinus pain and a black necrotic patch on the palate or nasal turbinate has Mucor or Rhizopus until proven otherwise.

highYield: Lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci in CSF from an adult point to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Meningococcal LOS endotoxin causes petechial rash, shock, and adrenal hemorrhage.
Hib conjugate vaccine turns the PRP capsule into a T-cell-dependent antigen that infants can respond to.
Listeria spreads cell to cell by actin tails and is linked to deli meats and unpasteurized cheese.
Botulinum gives descending flaccid paralysis; tetanus gives spastic paralysis with trismus.
Rabies travels retrograde along axons; a longer distance from bite to brain means a longer incubation.
Cryptococcus: India ink halo and capsular antigen test in CSF of a patient with AIDS.
Mycobacterium leprae invades Schwann cells and favors cool body sites.
pitfalls: Both meningococcus and gonococcus are gram-negative diplococci; only meningococcus has a polysaccharide capsule.
Listeria is a gram-positive rod; a gram-positive rod in neonatal CSF is Listeria, while cocci in chains point to group B Streptococcus.
Mucor has broad nonseptate hyphae with wide-angle branching; Aspergillus has narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles.
VDRL and RPR fall after treatment and can be falsely positive (pregnancy, lupus, some infections); FTA-ABS stays positive for life.
JC virus is latent in the kidney and damages oligodendrocytes; herpesviruses are latent in sensory ganglia.

N. meningitidis: gram-negative diplococci, capsule and LOS endotoxin, young adults in crowded living
Hib: gram-negative coccobacillus, PRP capsule, unvaccinated children
Group B Strep: gram-positive cocci in chains, maternal colonization, neonates
E. coli K1: gram-negative rod, K1 capsule, neonates
Listeria: gram-positive rod, tumbling motility, actin tails, deli meats and soft cheese
Capsules block phagocytosis and complement

summary: Neurological vascular disease covers stroke from blocked or bursting vessels, brain injury from global loss of blood flow, bleeding inside the skull, and loss of blood supply to the spinal cord. Exams test the mechanism behind each lesion, where it sits, how it looks under the microscope over time, and what complication follows.

points: Thrombotic infarct: a clot forms on an atherosclerotic plaque, most often at the carotid bifurcation, the middle cerebral artery, or the basilar artery.
Embolic infarct: a clot travels from the heart (atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus after MI, valve disease) or a carotid plaque, usually into the MCA; reperfusion often turns it hemorrhagic.
Lacunar infarct: hypertensive arteriolosclerosis narrows small penetrating (lenticulostriate) arteries, leaving small cavities in the basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus, or pons.
TIA: brief focal deficit, usually gone within an hour, with no infarct on imaging; a warning sign for stroke.
Shared risk factors: hypertension (the strongest), atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia.
Noncontrast CT comes first because fresh blood is bright on CT right away, while early ischemia may not show for hours; hemorrhage must be excluded before clot-dissolving therapy.

notes.h: What an infarct looks like over time
points: About 12 to 24 hours: red neurons (shrunken, eosinophilic cytoplasm, dark pyknotic nuclei).
About 1 to 3 days: neutrophils enter.
From about day 3 to weeks: macrophages (microglia) eat the debris.
Weeks to months: reactive astrocytes form gliosis around a fluid-filled cyst, the end result of liquefactive necrosis.
Cardiac arrest, shock, drowning, or carbon monoxide cut oxygen to the whole brain; glutamate excitotoxicity and calcium influx kill neurons.
Most vulnerable neurons: hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, and neocortical pyramidal cells (laminar necrosis in layers 3, 5, and 6).
Severe hypotension causes watershed infarcts in border zones between arterial territories, such as between the ACA and MCA (proximal arm and shoulder weakness).
Epidural hematoma: temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery; brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline; biconvex and stopped by sutures.
Subdural hematoma: tearing of bridging veins with brain atrophy (older adults, alcohol use) or shaking (infants); crescent-shaped and crosses sutures.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage: a saccular (berry) aneurysm ruptures, most often at the anterior communicating artery; sudden worst headache of life, neck stiffness, xanthochromic CSF.
Aneurysm risk: ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, smoking, hypertension. After SAH: rebleeding, vasospasm with delayed infarcts (about days 3 to 14), and hydrocephalus.
Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms burst in the basal ganglia (putamen), thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy: beta-amyloid in walls of cortical vessels causes recurrent lobar hemorrhage in older adults.
Arteriovenous malformation: tangled arteries drain straight into veins with no capillary bed; causes hemorrhage and seizures in young adults.

Carotid or vertebral dissection: an intimal tear after neck trauma lets blood into the wall, narrowing the lumen and seeding emboli; stroke in a young adult with neck pain (Horner syndrome with carotid dissection).

Subclavian steal: stenosis of the subclavian artery before the vertebral branch; arm exercise pulls blood backward down the vertebral artery, causing arm claudication, dizziness, and lower blood pressure in that arm.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: hypercoagulable states (pregnancy, postpartum, estrogen) clot the dural sinuses; headache, papilledema, seizures, hemorrhagic venous infarcts.

Hypertensive encephalopathy and PRES: severe hypertension overwhelms autoregulation, the blood-brain barrier leaks, and vasogenic edema forms, mainly in posterior (parieto-occipital) white matter; headache, confusion, vision loss, seizures; usually reversible.
Spinal cord supply: one anterior spinal artery (front two-thirds of the cord) and two posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns); the artery of Adamkiewicz feeds the lower cord.
Anterior spinal artery syndrome after aortic surgery or dissection: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, bladder loss, with vibration and position sense spared.

rows: Reactive gliosis around a fluid-filled cyst (liquefactive necrosis)

tricks.label: Epidural artery, subdural vein
tricks.text: Arterial bleeding is fast, so epidural patients crash after a lucid interval. Venous bleeding is slow, so subdural bleeds can build over days to weeks in older adults.

tricks.label: Shape follows the dura
tricks.text: Epidural blood must peel the dura off the skull, and sutures hold the dura down, so it bulges into a lens. Subdural blood spreads freely under the dura and crosses sutures as a crescent.

tricks.label: Deep bleed or lobar bleed
tricks.text: Deep bleeds (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) point to hypertension. Lobar bleeds near the cortex in an older adult point to amyloid angiopathy.

tricks.label: Front of the cord
tricks.text: The anterior spinal artery feeds the front two-thirds of the cord, which is everything except the dorsal columns and the back of the dorsal horns. So a patient who can still feel vibration in the toes but cannot move or feel pinprick has lost the anterior spinal artery.

highYield: Embolic infarcts often turn hemorrhagic when the clot breaks up and blood reenters damaged vessels.
Lacunar infarcts come from hypertensive arteriolosclerosis of small penetrating arteries.
Red neurons appear about 12 to 24 hours after an infarct; the end stage is a cyst lined by gliosis.
Hippocampal CA1 neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells die first in global hypoxia.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage: worst headache of life, xanthochromia, then vasospasm days later.
ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome raise the risk of berry aneurysm.
Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares vibration and position sense.
PRES is reversible vasogenic edema of posterior white matter in severe hypertension or eclampsia.
pitfalls: A TIA leaves no infarct on imaging; a deficit with an infarct on MRI is a stroke even if it resolves.
Cytotoxic edema follows ischemia; PRES and hypertensive encephalopathy cause vasogenic edema.
The lucid interval belongs to epidural hematoma; a slow decline over weeks in an older adult points to chronic subdural hematoma.
Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms cause deep hypertensive bleeds; saccular berry aneurysms cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Watershed infarcts come from low perfusion pressure across the whole brain, while embolic infarcts sit inside one arterial territory.

dumps.p: Draw four skull cross-sections side by side showing an epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, and hypertensive intraparenchymal bleed. Label the vessel that bleeds, the shape on CT, and the classic patient for each.

Epidural: biconvex, limited by sutures, lucid interval
Subdural: bridging veins, older adults, alcohol use, shaken infants
Subdural: crescent that crosses sutures
Subarachnoid: ruptured berry aneurysm, often anterior communicating artery
Subarachnoid: blood in cisterns, xanthochromia, vasospasm, hydrocephalus
Intraparenchymal: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum

summary: This unit covers diseases where neurons slowly die (Alzheimer, ALS, Parkinson, Huntington, Friedreich ataxia, other dementias) and diseases where myelin is attacked (multiple sclerosis, ADEM, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre). Exams test the protein or gene behind each disease, the cells and tracts that are lost, and the signs that separate look-alikes.

points: Beta then gamma secretase cut amyloid precursor protein into amyloid beta, which clumps into extracellular plaques.
Hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular neurofibrillary tangles; tangle burden tracks with the degree of dementia.
Risks: age, APOE e4, Down syndrome (APP gene on chromosome 21), and early-onset familial APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations.
Gross: narrow gyri, wide sulci, and enlarged ventricles (hydrocephalus ex vacuo), worst in the hippocampus and temporal lobes.
Micro: neuritic plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid angiopathy; loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert.
Course: short-term memory loss first, then language and visuospatial problems, then full dependence.
Dementia with Lewy bodies: cortical alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies; visual hallucinations, fluctuating attention, and parkinsonism early.
Frontotemporal dementia: early personality change, disinhibition, or language loss, with memory spared early; tau Pick bodies or TDP-43 inclusions.
Progressive supranuclear palsy: tau disease with vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and early backward falls.
Vascular dementia: stepwise decline after multiple infarcts or diffuse small vessel disease, with hypertension and diabetes as risks.
Mild cognitive impairment: measurable decline beyond normal aging, with daily function still intact.
ALS: upper and lower motor neurons die together; weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations plus spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign.
ALS spares sensation, bladder control, and eye movements; familial cases involve SOD1 or C9orf72; death from respiratory failure.
Parkinson disease: loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies; resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability.
Secondary parkinsonism: MPTP (a street-drug contaminant converted by MAO-B into a nigral toxin) and dopamine-blocking drugs such as antipsychotics.
Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT on chromosome 4; caudate atrophy with loss of GABAergic neurons; chorea, dementia, depression in midlife.
Huntington shows anticipation: repeats expand further during spermatogenesis, so paternal transmission brings earlier onset.
Friedreich ataxia: autosomal recessive GAA expansion in frataxin; mitochondrial iron builds up and damages dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts.
Friedreich extras: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (main cause of death), diabetes, kyphoscoliosis, pes cavus.
Essential tremor: often familial, postural and action tremor of hands, head, or voice that may ease with alcohol. Cervical dystonia: sustained neck muscle contraction twisting the head (torticollis).
Multiple sclerosis: autoimmune T cells and antibodies attack CNS myelin; most common in women aged 20 to 40 and at higher latitude; usually relapsing-remitting.
MS findings: optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), sensory loss, weakness, bladder problems, and symptoms worse with heat (Uhthoff phenomenon).
MS tests: periventricular white matter plaques on MRI and oligoclonal IgG bands in CSF.
ADEM: one episode of widespread perivenular demyelination, mostly in children, after a viral infection or rarely a vaccine; encephalopathy is common.
Transverse myelitis: inflammation across one cord segment, after infection or with MS; bilateral weakness, a sensory level, and bladder dysfunction.
Guillain-Barre: after infection (Campylobacter jejuni, viruses), immune attack on peripheral myelin and roots; ascending symmetric flaccid weakness with lost reflexes.
Guillain-Barre complications: respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness and autonomic instability (arrhythmias, blood pressure swings); CSF has high protein with normal cell count.

tricks.label: TRAP (Parkinson disease)
tricks.text: Tremor at rest, Rigidity (cogwheel), Akinesia or bradykinesia, Postural instability.

tricks.label: SIN (Charcot triad of MS)
tricks.text: Scanning speech, Intention tremor, Nystagmus. It points to MS plaques in the cerebellar pathways.

tricks.label: ALS spares the eyes and bladder
tricks.text: ALS mixes UMN and LMN signs in the same limb while sensation, bladder control, and eye movements stay normal. A sensory level or bladder loss points elsewhere, such as cord compression.

tricks.label: One time versus many times
tricks.text: ADEM is one attack in a child after an infection. MS is many attacks over years in a young adult, with lesions of different ages.

highYield: APOE e4 raises late-onset Alzheimer risk; APP, PSEN1, and PSEN2 mutations cause early-onset familial disease.
Down syndrome patients develop Alzheimer changes early because the APP gene is on chromosome 21.
ALS is the classic disease with both UMN and LMN signs and no sensory loss.
Parkinson disease: Lewy bodies made of alpha-synuclein in the substantia nigra.
Huntington disease: CAG repeat on chromosome 4, caudate atrophy, anticipation through the father.
Friedreich ataxia patients most often die of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Guillain-Barre: high CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation).
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult points to MS.
pitfalls: Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra mean Parkinson disease; Lewy bodies spread through the cortex with early hallucinations mean dementia with Lewy bodies.
Pick bodies are tau inclusions of frontotemporal dementia; Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein.
Guillain-Barre attacks peripheral myelin (Schwann cells); MS and ADEM attack CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes).
Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive (GAA); Huntington disease is autosomal dominant (CAG).
Mild cognitive impairment leaves daily function intact; dementia means the person can no longer manage daily life alone.

l: Alzheimer: amyloid beta and tau, hippocampus and cortex, APOE e4 and APP or PSEN mutations, short-term memory loss
Parkinson: alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, substantia nigra dopamine neurons, TRAP signs
Huntington: HTT CAG repeat on chromosome 4, caudate GABA neurons, autosomal dominant, chorea and dementia
ALS: upper and lower motor neurons, SOD1 or C9orf72 in familial cases, mixed UMN and LMN signs
Friedreich: frataxin GAA repeat, dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts, autosomal recessive
Friedreich extras: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, kyphoscoliosis, pes cavus
Huntington anticipation through paternal transmission

summary: The skull cannot expand, so extra water in the brain (edema) or extra CSF (hydrocephalus) raises intracranial pressure. Exams test which type of edema goes with which cause, where CSF flow is blocked, and the signs of raised pressure and herniation.

points: Vasogenic edema: the blood-brain barrier leaks around a tumor, abscess, or injury; fluid collects mostly in white matter.
Cytotoxic edema: ischemia or hypoxia stops the Na+/K+ ATPase, sodium and water enter cells, and the cells swell.
Interstitial edema: in obstructive hydrocephalus, CSF is pushed across the ependyma into periventricular white matter.
Because the skull is a fixed box, added volume of brain, blood, or CSF quickly raises intracranial pressure.
Signs: headache worse lying down, vomiting, papilledema, and falling consciousness.
Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing; a late sign of brainstem compression.
Subfalcine herniation: cingulate gyrus slides under the falx and can compress the anterior cerebral artery.
Uncal herniation: medial temporal lobe compresses CN III (dilated pupil on the same side), the posterior cerebral artery, and the cerebral peduncle; brainstem stretching causes Duret hemorrhages.
Tonsillar herniation: cerebellar tonsils push through the foramen magnum and compress the medulla, stopping breathing.
Noncommunicating (obstructive): flow is blocked inside the ventricles, for example aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker malformation, or a tumor.
Communicating: CSF moves through the ventricles but is not absorbed, usually because arachnoid granulations are scarred after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo: ventricles look large only because brain tissue has been lost (Alzheimer, Huntington, other atrophy); pressure is normal.
In infants the skull sutures are open, so raised pressure enlarges the head; a bulging fontanelle and downward gaze (sunset eyes) may appear.
Chiari II: cerebellar vermis and tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele. Dandy-Walker: absent or small vermis with a cystic fourth ventricle.
Older adults; enlarged ventricles with opening pressure that is not consistently high.
Stretched periventricular fibers cause urinary incontinence, a broad shuffling magnetic gait, and dementia.
Symptoms, especially gait, may improve after removing CSF by lumbar puncture, which predicts benefit from a shunt.
Classic patient: obese woman of childbearing age.
Headache, papilledema, transient vision loss, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia from CN VI palsy.
Imaging is normal (no mass, no hydrocephalus); opening pressure is high, above about 25 cm H2O (normal about 10 to 20), with normal CSF content.
Associations: excess vitamin A and tetracyclines.
The main complication is permanent vision loss from optic nerve damage.

charts.title: Increased intracranial fluid by condition

tricks.label: Wet, wobbly, and wacky (NPH)
tricks.text: Wet: urinary incontinence. Wobbly: magnetic gait. Wacky: dementia.

tricks.label: CN VI is a false localizer
tricks.text: The abducens nerve runs a long path along the skull base, so any rise in intracranial pressure can stretch it. A CN VI palsy in IIH does not mean a lesion sits near the nerve.

tricks.label: Blown pupil first
tricks.text: Pupillary fibers run on the outside of CN III, so the first sign of uncal compression is a dilated, sluggish pupil on the side of the mass.

highYield: Vasogenic edema surrounds tumors and abscesses; cytotoxic edema follows ischemia.
Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing.
Uncal herniation compresses CN III and gives a dilated pupil on the same side.
Aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of congenital noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
Scarred arachnoid granulations after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage cause communicating hydrocephalus.
NPH: incontinence, magnetic gait, dementia, improving after CSF removal.
IIH: obese young woman, papilledema, CN VI palsy, normal imaging, high opening pressure.
pitfalls: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo has large ventricles from brain loss and normal pressure; true hydrocephalus is a CSF flow or absorption problem.
Communicating means CSF can pass between ventricles and subarachnoid space; the problem is absorption.
IIH has normal imaging, so large ventricles on CT point away from IIH.
Papilledema means raised intracranial pressure and is usually bilateral; one swollen disc with pain on eye movement points to optic neuritis.

summary: Metabolic and nutritional problems injure the brain and nerves: ammonia in liver failure, high glucose in diabetes, missing B12 or thiamine, and too-fast sodium correction. Inherited neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth) is included. Exams test the biochemical cause, which tracts or nerves are hit, and the pattern of findings.

points: Gut bacteria make ammonia; in cirrhosis or a portosystemic shunt it bypasses the liver and reaches the brain.
Astrocytes clear ammonia by making glutamine, which builds up and swells them.
Precipitants: GI bleeding (a protein load), infection, high protein intake, constipation, hypokalemia, and sedatives.
Hypokalemia raises kidney ammonia production.
Findings: confusion, day-night reversal, asterixis (flapping hands with wrists extended), and coma in severe cases.
Distal symmetric (stocking-glove): longest nerves fail first; diabetes, alcohol, B12 and thiamine deficiency, HIV, and chemotherapy (vincristine, taxanes, cisplatin).
Mononeuropathy: one nerve, from compression (carpal tunnel) or ischemia (diabetic CN III palsy).
Mononeuritis multiplex: several named nerves in a patchy pattern, from vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa) or leprosy.
Axonal injury lowers signal amplitude on nerve conduction and recovers slowly; demyelinating injury slows conduction velocity.
Aldose reductase turns excess glucose into sorbitol in Schwann cells, drawing in water and using up NADPH.
Advanced glycation end products and microvascular disease of the vasa nervorum add to nerve injury.
Findings: stocking-glove loss of pain, temperature, and vibration, with lost ankle reflexes.
Autonomic loss: gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, and bladder retention.
Painless pressure injuries cause neuropathic foot ulcers under the metatarsal heads.
Pupil-sparing CN III palsy: ischemia hits the core of the nerve, while the outer pupillary fibers keep their blood supply.
Causes: pernicious anemia (antibodies to parietal cells or intrinsic factor), strict vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection, Diphyllobothrium latum.
B12 is needed for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise.
Subacute combined degeneration hits the dorsal columns (lost vibration and position sense, positive Romberg sign) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity, Babinski sign).
Peripheral neuropathy and dementia can occur, even without anemia.
Wernicke encephalopathy: thiamine deficiency in alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, or hyperemesis; confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia.
Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, so energy-hungry brain areas fail; glucose given before thiamine can trigger an attack.
Korsakoff syndrome: lasting amnesia with confabulation; damage in the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.
Osmotic demyelination: chronic hyponatremia corrected too fast (more than about 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours) shrinks brain cells and destroys myelin in the central pons.
Osmotic demyelination signs appear days later: quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and possible locked-in syndrome.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth: inherited motor and sensory neuropathy, most often autosomal dominant PMP22 duplication; distal weakness, foot drop, pes cavus, hammer toes.

tricks.label: From low to high, your pons will die
tricks.text: Raising sodium too fast in chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination of the pons. The reverse, from high to low, your brain will blow: lowering sodium too fast in hypernatremia causes cerebral edema.

tricks.label: Pupil tells the cause
tricks.text: Diabetic CN III palsy spares the pupil because ischemia hits the core of the nerve. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm presses on the outside first, so the pupil dilates.

tricks.label: B12 or folate
tricks.text: Both raise homocysteine and cause megaloblastic anemia. Only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid and damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts.

tricks.label: Thiamine before glucose
tricks.text: Glucose pushes more fuel through thiamine-dependent enzymes. Giving it first to a thiamine-deficient patient can set off Wernicke encephalopathy.

highYield: Hypokalemia, GI bleeding, infection, and constipation all raise ammonia and can trigger hepatic encephalopathy.
Asterixis is the classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
Diabetic neuropathy: sorbitol buildup, advanced glycation end products, and microvascular injury.
Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns plus lateral corticospinal tracts, with a positive Romberg sign.
Wernicke triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; mammillary bodies are damaged.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A comes from PMP22 duplication and gives foot drop and pes cavus.
Osmotic demyelination follows overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia.
pitfalls: B12 deficiency can damage the nervous system without anemia, especially when folate intake is high.
Wernicke encephalopathy is acute and can reverse with thiamine; Korsakoff amnesia is chronic and mostly permanent.
Mononeuritis multiplex is several separate named nerves; distal symmetric neuropathy is a stocking-glove pattern.
Asterixis also appears in uremia and CO2 retention, so it supports hepatic encephalopathy only alongside liver disease.

summary: Many inherited and congenital diseases injure the developing brain: chromosomal disorders, enzyme defects that let toxic substances build up, storage diseases, and infections or toxins before birth. Exams test the missing enzyme or gene, what accumulates, how it is inherited, and the clue that tells similar diseases apart.

points: Down syndrome (trisomy 21): intellectual disability, hypotonia, flat face, upslanting eyes, single palmar crease.
Early-onset Alzheimer disease, because the APP gene is on chromosome 21.
Atlantoaxial instability can compress the spinal cord.
Associated: duodenal atresia, atrioventricular septal defect, and higher leukemia risk.
Fragile X: CGG expansion in FMR1 leads to hypermethylation and silencing; the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.
Fragile X findings: autism features, long face, large jaw and ears, macroorchidism after puberty.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: ABCD1 defect blocks very long chain fatty acid entry into peroxisomes for oxidation; they build up in white matter and the adrenal cortex; boys with behavior change, vision loss, and adrenal insufficiency.
Metachromatic leukodystrophy: autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency; sulfatides build up and destroy central and peripheral myelin.
Krabbe disease: autosomal recessive galactocerebrosidase deficiency; psychosine kills myelin-forming cells; multinucleated globoid cells; infants with irritability, spasticity, and neuropathy.

notes.h: Amino acid and urea cycle disorders
points: PKU: autosomal recessive phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (or loss of its cofactor BH4); tyrosine becomes essential.
PKU signs: intellectual disability, seizures, musty odor, fair skin and hair (less melanin), eczema.
Maternal PKU: high phenylalanine in an untreated mother causes microcephaly, intellectual disability, and heart defects in the baby.
Maple syrup urine disease: branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency; leucine, isoleucine, and valine build up; sweet urine odor, poor feeding, seizures in the newborn.
OTC deficiency: X-linked; carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid rises; hyperammonemia causes vomiting, lethargy, and cerebral edema in newborn boys.
Tay-Sachs: hexosaminidase A deficiency, GM2 ganglioside; progressive neurodegeneration, exaggerated startle, cherry-red macula, no hepatosplenomegaly.
Niemann-Pick: sphingomyelinase deficiency; neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, hepatosplenomegaly, foamy macrophages.
Fabry: X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency; burning pain in hands and feet, angiokeratomas, decreased sweating, early stroke, kidney and heart disease.
Gaucher: glucocerebrosidase deficiency; type 1 spares the brain, types 2 and 3 are neuronopathic.
Hurler: alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency with corneal clouding; Hunter: X-linked iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, milder, no corneal clouding.

Acute intermittent porphyria: autosomal dominant porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency; abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms, high urine porphobilinogen; triggered by alcohol, fasting, and CYP450 inducers.
Wilson disease: autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation; copper is not excreted into bile or loaded onto ceruloplasmin, so serum ceruloplasmin is low.
Copper in the basal ganglia causes tremor, dystonia, and psychiatric change; copper in Descemet membrane makes Kayser-Fleischer rings; liver disease from hepatitis to cirrhosis.
Congenital microcephaly: Zika, CMV, rubella, and toxoplasma infection in pregnancy, fetal alcohol syndrome, and maternal PKU.

tricks.label: Hunters see clearly and aim for the X
tricks.text: Hunter syndrome has no corneal clouding (see clearly) and is X-linked. Hurler has corneal clouding and is autosomal recessive.

tricks.label: I Love Vermont maple syrup
tricks.text: Isoleucine, Leucine, Valine build up in maple syrup urine disease.

tricks.label: CGG: Chin, Giant Gonads
tricks.text: Fragile X is a CGG repeat; long face with a large jaw and macroorchidism.

tricks.label: Cherry-red spot plus organs
tricks.text: Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick both give a cherry-red macula. A big liver and spleen point to Niemann-Pick; a normal-sized liver and spleen point to Tay-Sachs.

highYield: Down syndrome: early Alzheimer disease from the extra APP gene, atlantoaxial instability, AV septal defect, duodenal atresia.
Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: very long chain fatty acids, white matter loss, and adrenal insufficiency.
PKU makes tyrosine essential; less tyrosine means less melanin and fair skin.
OTC deficiency raises orotic acid and ammonia without megaloblastic anemia.
Acute intermittent porphyria attacks are triggered by alcohol, fasting, and CYP450 inducers.
Wilson disease: low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia and liver damage.
Fabry disease causes painful neuropathy and early stroke in young men.
pitfalls: Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability, but it is rarely inherited; fragile X is the most common inherited cause.
X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is a peroxisomal disorder; metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease are lysosomal.
OTC deficiency gives orotic aciduria with hyperammonemia; UMP synthase deficiency gives orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anemia and normal ammonia.
Acute intermittent porphyria has no photosensitivity, unlike porphyria cutanea tarda.
Wilson disease has low ceruloplasmin; serum copper can be low or normal even though tissue copper is high.
